# Where we are

## Recap

Thursday we asked what experience is *of*.

- Russell's answer was **sense-data**: private objects you're immediately aware of.
- One rival said experience **represents** the world, the way a sentence does.
- The other said you're aware of the **thing itself**, and looking a certain way is something the thing does.

. . .

Three answers, one question. What is experience directed at?

## A different question

Today we change the question.

Not what your experience is *of*, but what it is *like*.

. . .

And then a harder one. How much can you find out about what somebody else's experience is like?

## Thomas Nagel

Thomas Nagel, born 1937, has spent most of his career at NYU.

"What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" came out in 1974 and is one of the most cited papers in modern philosophy.

. . .

It's also one of the shortest and plainest, and those two facts are not unrelated.

# Consciousness

## The thing that makes it hard

Nagel's complaint is that people writing on the mind-body problem keep making it look tractable, and that they manage this by leaving out the part that isn't.

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
Consciousness is what makes the mind-body problem really intractable.
::::

## What he means by it

Not self-awareness. Not intelligence. Not the ability to report on yourself.

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
[F]undamentally an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something that it is like to be that organism---something it is like *for* the organism.
::::

. . .

That last clause is load-bearing. Not something it is like *to us*, or from outside. Something it is like for the thing itself.

## A trap in the English

"What is it like to be a bat?" sounds like a request for a comparison. *Oh, it's a bit like being a small dog with bad eyesight.*

. . .

That's not the question, and the grammar misleads here. The "like" isn't comparative.

The question is whether there is any way things seem from in there. Whether the lights are on.

## Why bats

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
I have chosen bats instead of wasps or flounders because if one travels too far down the phylogenetic tree, people gradually shed their faith that there is experience there at all.
::::

. . .

Bats are mammals. Almost nobody wants to say there's nothing going on in there.

But the way they find out about the world is nothing like ours.

## Sonar

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
[B]at sonar, though clearly a form of perception, is not similar in its operation to any sense that we possess, and there is no reason to suppose that it is subjectively like anything we can experience or imagine.
::::

## iClicker QUIZ

Nagel says he picked bats rather than wasps or flounders. Why?

A.  Bats are mammals, so we're more confident there's experience there at all
B.  Bat sonar has been studied more carefully than insect senses
C.  Bats are more intelligent than wasps or flounders
D.  Bats are nocturnal, so their experience is more unlike ours

# Imagination

## Try it

Imagine you have webbing on your arms. Imagine catching insects in your mouth. Imagine spending the day hanging upside down in an attic, and the night flying around in the dark.

. . .

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
In so far as I can imagine this (which is not very far), it tells me only what it would be like for *me* to behave as a bat behaves. But that is not the question. I want to know what it is like for a *bat* to be a bat.
::::

## Why the test fails

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
Our own experience provides the basic material for our imagination, whose range is therefore limited.
::::

. . .

You can add to what you've had, subtract from it, or rearrange it. What you can't do is start from somewhere else.

## It isn't really about bats

The bat is vivid, but the point is general, and it runs much closer to home.

The same problem arises between a person blind from birth and a sighted person, and for all we know between any two of us.

. . .

And it runs in the other direction too. Intelligent bats might come to know far more about human brains than we ever will, and still be unable to form any conception of what it is like to be us.

# Objectivity

## Point of view

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
[E]very subjective phenomenon is essentially connected with a single point of view, and it seems inevitable that an objective, physical theory will abandon that point of view.
::::

## The reversal

This is the move that makes the paper more than a good example.

Normally, getting more objective gets you *closer* to how things are. You drop your parochial vantage point and you see the thing as it is.

. . .

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
If the subjective character of experience is fully comprehensible only from one point of view, then any shift to greater objectivity---that is, less attachment to a specific viewpoint---does not take us nearer to the real nature of the phenomenon: it takes us farther away from it.
::::

## What physics does

Physics works by subtracting the point of view.

Colour as you see it goes; wavelength stays. Warmth as you feel it goes; mean kinetic energy stays. Every step is a success, and every step drops something tied to being a particular perceiver in a particular place.

. . .

The trouble is that the thing we're now trying to explain is exactly the bit that keeps getting dropped.

## A quick question (POLL)

Suppose bat neuroscience is finished. Every neuron mapped, every process understood, nothing left over.

**Would we then know what it is like to be a bat?**

A.  Yes. There'd be nothing left to know
B.  No, and that shows the physical story leaves something out
C.  No, but only because we couldn't *imagine* it. Nothing is left out of the story
D.  The question has no answer

. . .

Hold on to your answer. B and C are the whole debate, and Thursday is about how to tell them apart.

## What Nagel is not saying

This is the part that gets misreported, including by people who like the conclusion.

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
It would be a mistake to conclude that physicalism must be false.
::::

. . .

His claim is weaker, and stranger. It's that we don't properly understand what physicalism is asserting, because *we do not at present have any conception of how it might be true*.

## Objective phenomenology

He doesn't stop at the complaint. He sketches a programme.

The idea is a way of describing experience that doesn't depend on being able to have it --- the way a person blind from birth can understand a great deal about what sighted people are up to.

:::: {.callout-note title="Nagel"}
[A] phenomenology that is in this sense objective may permit questions about the physical basis of experience to assume a more intelligible form.
::::

. . .

He does not say how to build one. Fifty years later, nor has anyone else.

# Thought and feeling

## What the argument didn't need

Notice what never came up.

Nothing in the bat argument said bats are clever. Nothing said they reason, or plan, or have concepts. The argument works whether or not any of that is true.

. . .

All it needed was that there's something it is like to be one.

## Two different things

Thinking
:    Whatever it is we do with our observations of the world, and with combinations of them. Reasoning, planning, inferring. Humans do it; thermostats don't.

Consciousness
:    There being something it is like, for the thing itself.

. . .

These are two concepts, not one. Any connection between them needs an argument, and nobody gets to slide from one to the other without giving one.

## Why it's worth saying out loud

Ordinary speech runs them together, and so does a lot of the current argument about machines. *Does it really think?* and *is there anything it's like to be it?* get asked as though they were the same question.

. . .

They're not. Keeping them apart is one of the things this unit is for, and we'll do it properly next Tuesday.

## Thursday

Nagel says we can't see how a physical story could capture what experience is like.

. . .

Thursday we look at an argument that tries to turn that into a proof: not just that we can't see how physicalism could be true, but that it isn't.

The case is a scientist who knows everything there is to know about colour vision, and has never seen a colour.
